title: Plasticity modelling for deformation-induced anisotropy in sheet metals: from experiments to finite element implementation
abstract: Abstract Deformation-induced anisotropic hardening strongly influences springback, strain localisation, forming limits and unloading-sensitive response in metallic sheet materials, and must therefore be represented reliably in finite-element simulations of sheet-forming operations. Existing syntheses have clarified the phenomenology of load-path effects and catalogued broad classes of constitutive models, but they have generally devoted less attention to the practical questions that govern engineering adoption: which observed behaviours justify which model family, what test information is minimally required for calibration, and what implementation burden follows at the FE level. This article presents a critical narrative review of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening in metallic sheet materials from the viewpoint of model selection, calibration and finite-element deployment. Experimentally observed responses are reorganised into a three-layer framework linking observable hardening signatures, constitutive evolution modes and representative model families. Prior syntheses are positioned explicitly to define the distinct contribution of the present review in terms of calibration burden, identifiability, implementation readiness and decision-oriented model choice. Crystal-plasticity-based approaches are discussed as supporting virtual laboratories for mechanism interpretation and synthetic calibration data generation. Computational issues relevant to industrial deployment are reviewed in terms of local stress updates, consistent elastoplastic tangents and parameter-identification workflows. The scope is restricted to constitutive descriptions of anisotropy evolution in metallic sheet materials up to the onset of localised necking. The overall aim is to provide a practical map for choosing, calibrating and implementing anisotropic hardening models in sheet-forming simulations.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Lightweight metallic sheet materials such as advanced high-strength steels and aluminium alloys are now standard in automotive and transportation structures, driven by the combined requirements of weight reduction, crash performance and sustainability [ 2 ]. Their macroscopic behaviour is strongly anisotropic as a result of processing-induced texture, microstructure and residual stress fields, as documented in numerous experimental and modelling studies on sheet anisotropy and its evolution during forming [ 3 ,  4 ]. In industrial applications, deformation-induced changes of plastic anisotropy have a first-order influence on springback, strain localisation and forming limits, and they are therefore a central concern in the design of forming processes and structural components [ 5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Furthermore, the integration of such constitutive models into process design and die-face engineering has been demonstrated in various stamping applications [ 8 ]. Capturing these effects in a robust yet computationally efficient manner remains a key challenge in constitutive modelling and finite-element (FE) analysis.

From a phenomenological viewpoint, deformation-induced anisotropic hardening behaviours are often rationalised in terms of combined isotropic, kinematic and distortional hardening, as reflected in a broad range of yield criteria and hardening laws proposed over the last decades [ 10 ,  11 ,  12 – 13 ]. These macroscopic models remain attractive for large-scale FE simulations because they can, in principle, be calibrated from mechanical tests that are still compatible with engineering development cycles. At the same time, the proliferation of model variants and parameter sets has made it increasingly difficult for practitioners to decide which constitutive ingredients are actually required for a given sheet-metal problem, which tests are minimally necessary for identification, and which models remain numerically robust when transferred from academic benchmarks to industrial FE workflows. Extensive experimental campaigns have documented these issues for a wide range of alloys, including aluminium sheets and advanced high-strength steels [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ].

Crystal-plasticity (CP) models offer a complementary, microstructure-based description of anisotropy by explicitly resolving slip activity at the grain scale. Modern CP and crystal-plasticity finite element (CPFE) frameworks account for texture, grain morphology and microstructure evolution and are capable of predicting evolving yield loci,  r -values and tension–compression asymmetries from underlying slip and hardening mechanisms [ 19 ,  20 ]. Mean-field and full-field CP simulations have been used to study anisotropy evolution in steels and aluminium alloys, including the role of processing routes and ageing treatments on sheet formability [ 21 ,  22 ]. However, despite their physical fidelity, CP-based models remain computationally demanding and are not yet the default choice for routine industrial forming simulations. In practice, CP models are often used as “virtual laboratories” to explore mechanisms and generate synthetic data, while macroscopic phenomenological models remain the workhorse in commercial FE codes.

sections.heading: Positioning relative to prior syntheses and reference texts
paragraphs: The literature relevant to the present topic already contains several important syntheses, but their centres of gravity are not identical. Broad reference texts have established the basis of sheet anisotropy, formability testing and constitutive modelling in metal forming [ 4 ,  7 ]. Review papers have examined testing and formability issues in sheet forming [ 25 ], advances in anisotropy and formability of sheet metals [ 24 ], and, most directly, phenomenological descriptions of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening [ 1 ]. CP and CPFE overview texts, while not reviews of sheet-hardening models in the narrow sense, provide the multiscale background needed to interpret anisotropy evolution mechanistically [ 19 ,  20 ]. Together, these sources have clarified the phenomenology of the field and documented a wide range of model families, experiments and applications.

sections.heading: Scope and review logic
paragraphs: This article is a critical narrative review rather than a systematic database-driven survey. Its aim is not to provide an exhaustive bibliometric census of every model variant, but to organise the literature in a form that is useful for constitutive choice, calibration and FE deployment. Accordingly, literature selection was guided by four streams: (i) experimental studies that reveal path-dependent anisotropic hardening in sheet metals; (ii) representative phenomenological model families that have become reference points for isotropic, kinematic, distortional and mixed hardening; (iii) CP and CPFE contributions used to interpret mechanisms or to generate synthetic calibration data; and (iv) computational sources on return mapping, consistent tangents and parameter-identification practice. Within each stream, priority is given to seminal papers, benchmark contributions and later studies that materially changed engineering practice, rather than to exhaustive enumeration of minor variants.

The scope is limited to metallic sheet materials and to constitutive descriptions of plastic anisotropy evolution up to the onset of localised necking. The review centres on macroscopic models that can be deployed in nonlinear FE simulations of forming, unloading and springback-sensitive processes. Ductile damage, fracture and forming-limit methodologies are discussed only when necessary to clarify the hardening backbone, and full CP framework development is included only insofar as it informs phenomenological modelling, calibration or interpretation [ 27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 – 31 ]. Likewise, application examples are used to expose model-selection and implementation trade-offs rather than to provide a sector-by-sector survey of forming operations. The intended contribution is therefore a decision-oriented engineering synthesis, not a replacement for dedicated texts on fracture, formability or multiscale crystal plasticity.

Several limitations follow directly from this scope. The tables and model maps proposed below should be read as decision aids, not as a universal ranking of constitutive models. No new experimental database is introduced, and the conclusions therefore concern the interpretation, selection and implementation of existing model families. In addition, CP-derived virtual data are useful only under the texture, boundary-condition, slip-law, hardening and RVE assumptions used to generate them; they should constrain and test phenomenological models rather than be treated as unconditional replacement data.

In particular, the review seeks to position the present contribution relative to prior syntheses and clarify its engineering focus on model selection, calibration and FE deployment; reorganise experimental manifestations of deformation-induced anisotropy into a taxonomy that is directly usable for model assessment and selection, including Bauschinger effects, cross-hardening, yield-surface distortion and path-dependent  r -value evolution; map this taxonomy onto representative phenomenological yield criteria and hardening laws, highlighting constitutive ingredients, parameter interpretation, identifiability and calibration requirements for realistic mechanical test programmes; clarify how crystal plasticity can act as a “virtual laboratory” for informing and constraining phenomenological models, for example by providing synthetic yield loci and  r -value data under complex loading paths; and discuss computational implementation and parameter-identification strategies that are crucial for FE robustness and industrial adoption, including local stress-update algorithms and consistent elastoplastic tangents for anisotropic hardening models. The paper is organised as follows. Section “ Experimental manifestations of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening ” summarises the main experimental manifestations of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening in sheet metals, including Bauschinger effects, cross-hardening, distortional evolution of the yield surface and path-dependent  r -value changes, together with the mechanical tests used to reveal these behaviours. On this basis, Section “ Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families ” introduces a taxonomy of hardening behaviours that serves as a unifying framework for comparing different constitutive models and for constructing model-selection maps. Section “ Phenomenological models for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening ” surveys representative phenomenological yield criteria and hardening laws, emphasising their mathematical structure, parameter sets and typical calibration strategies in the context of industrial sheet metals. Section “ Crystal-plasticity-based approaches and links to phenomenological models ” outlines selected crystal-plasticity approaches and discusses how they can inform or complement phenomenological descriptions of anisotropy evolution. Section “ Computational aspects for FE implementation ” addresses computational aspects relevant for FE implementation, including local stress-update algorithms, consistent elastoplastic tangents, convergence issues associated with non-smooth yield loci, and recent developments in parameter-identification strategies for anisotropic models. Finally, Section “ Synthesis: engineering takeaways, persistent debates and research priorities ” synthesises the discussion in terms of key themes, opposing viewpoints and research gaps, before the conclusions highlight promising directions for future research and industrial adoption.

sections.heading: Experimental manifestations of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening
paragraphs: Plastic deformation in metallic sheet materials exhibits several distinct manifestations of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening. Beyond the familiar evolution of flow stress with accumulated plastic strain, experiments reveal pronounced Bauschinger effects, cross-hardening and path-dependent r-values, as well as distortional changes of the yield locus under non-proportional loading [ 1 ,  7 ,  32 ]. These behaviours are strongly influenced by the material class (e.g. dual-phase steels, TRIP and TWIP steels, aluminium alloys) and by prior thermo-mechanical processing, and have direct implications for springback, forming limits and crash performance [ 25 ,  33 ]. No single mechanical test can expose all of these features; instead, a combination of targeted loading paths is required to isolate and quantify different aspects of anisotropy evolution [ 4 ,  24 ,  25 ].

Broadly speaking, uniaxial tensile tests in multiple in-plane directions provide information on initial planar anisotropy and its early evolution with plastic strain. Plane-strain tension and in-plane shear tests are used to probe the shape of the yield locus in specific stress states, while hydraulic bulge and cruciform tests supply data in the biaxial tension regime and underpin forming-limit characterisation [ 4 ,  7 ,  9 ,  23 ]. Early experimental investigations by Naghdi and Rowley [ 34 ] and Wu and Yeh [ 35 ] laid the groundwork for understanding yield surface distortion, while more recent yield-surface tracing techniques summarised by Stefan and co-workers [ 36 ] have refined the measurement of initial and evolving surfaces under combined loads. Theoretical frameworks for anisotropic hardening date back to Baltov and Sawczuk [ 37 ]. Reverse loading and cyclic tension–compression tests are essential to quantify the Bauschinger effect, transient hardening/softening after load reversal and cyclic stabilisation behaviour [ 10 ,  32 ,  38 ,  48 ,  49 ]. Finally, non-proportional and multi-step loading paths, including tension–shear combinations and multi-axial loading of thin-walled tubes, are required to reveal cross-hardening, path-dependent distortional hardening and complex yield surface evolution that cannot be inferred from proportional tests alone [ 1 ,  32 ]. Figure  1  and Table  2  summarise representative experimental configurations and highlight their main observables and modelling relevance. Fig. 1 Overview of experimental setups commonly used to characterise deformation-induced anisotropic hardening in sheet and tubular metallic materials [ 1 ,  4 ,  7 ,  25 ,  32 ]. The configurations shown correspond to the main test families listed in Table  2  and target different combinations of stress state, loading path and strain range, thereby revealing complementary aspects of anisotropy evolution

sections.heading: Summary of experimental tests and identified quantities
paragraphs: The experimental techniques discussed above provide complementary information on deformation-induced anisotropy. For constitutive model calibration and validation it is useful to view them not only in terms of specimen geometry but also in terms of the primary observables they deliver and the aspects of anisotropy and hardening that they constrain. Table  2  summarises representative test types used for steels and aluminium alloys, alongside the main measured quantities and the phenomena that each test is best suited to reveal [ 4 ,  7 ,  25 ].

From a modelling perspective, uniaxial tension tests at multiple in-plane orientations remain the backbone for determining initial planar anisotropy, basic isotropic hardening and the evolution of directional yield stresses and r-values with plastic strain [ 4 ,  24 ]. Plane-strain tension and in-plane shear tests provide essential constraints on the shape of the yield locus in tension and shear and on the ability of non-quadratic yield functions to reproduce the relative magnitudes of tensile and shear yield stresses [ 7 ,  23 ,  39 ]. Biaxial tests, including hydraulic bulge and cruciform configurations, probe the biaxial portion of the yield locus using cruciform specimens [ 40 ,  41 ] or tube expansion techniques [ 14 ,  15 ,  42 ]. Regarding strain-path changes, double-path experiments by Vincze et al. [ 43 ,  44 ] and Rauch et al. [ 45 ] have been instrumental in classifying transient hardening behaviors. Additionally, forming limit characterisation under complex strain paths has been detailed by Iizuka et al. [ 46 ] and Butuc et al. [ 47 ], highlighting the strong influence of pre-strain on limit strains.

In summary, the tests in Table  2  should be viewed as a staged calibration toolbox rather than as an exhaustive mandatory programme. Section “ Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families ” reorganises these observables into a taxonomy linking test evidence to constitutive model families and FE-oriented model selection.

sections.heading: Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families
paragraphs: A recurring difficulty in reviews of deformation-induced anisotropic hardening is that three levels of description are often blended together: experimentally observed phenomena (for example Bauschinger-type responses, cross-hardening and path-dependent  r -values), idealised constitutive evolution modes (isotropic expansion, kinematic translation, distortional shape change, evolving anisotropy coefficients), and named model families that implement those modes. For model selection and FE implementation, these levels should be kept distinct. A given phenomenon can often be reproduced by more than one constitutive descriptor, while a single model family may cover several phenomena at once. The taxonomy proposed here is therefore organised row-wise by the dominant  observed phenomenon , and column-wise by the  constitutive descriptor(s)  and  representative model families  most commonly used to reproduce it, together with the minimum sensible test information required for calibration and validation [ 11 ,  51 ,  53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 ].

This separation matters operationally. Experimentalists first see signatures in stress–strain curves, yield loci and  r -values; constitutive analysts then decide which internal variables and evolution terms are needed; FE analysts finally judge whether a given model family can be identified, integrated and deployed with acceptable robustness and cost. The purpose of the present taxonomy is to make these transitions explicit and to avoid the common but misleading impression that one observed hardening phenomenon implies a unique constitutive structure or a unique model family.

At the level of constitutive descriptors, the most common idealised modes of yield-locus evolution remain isotropic, kinematic, distortional and mixed evolution. Isotropic evolution denotes an approximately uniform expansion or contraction of the locus driven by scalar measures of accumulated plastic deformation. Kinematic evolution denotes translation of an approximately shape-invariant locus through one or more backstress-like variables. Distortional evolution denotes path-dependent changes in locus shape and curvature. Mixed descriptions combine these ingredients and, in many modern sheet-metal formulations, may be supplemented by explicit evolution laws for anisotropy coefficients or other path descriptors. Cross-hardening and strongly non-proportional effects should therefore be viewed primarily as  observed loading-path phenomena , not as stand-alone descriptor classes; they generally require mixed constitutive structures with directional or history-dependent internal variables [ 1 ,  10 ,  32 ,  38 ,  55 ,  57 ,  58 ].

sections.heading: Three-layer decomposition and yield locus evolution
paragraphs: The distinction between observed phenomena and constitutive descriptors can be illustrated most simply in one dimension. In Fig.  2 , the response of a material subjected to monotonic tension up to a maximum strain, followed by reverse loading in compression, is sketched schematically. The  observed phenomenon  is the Bauschinger effect, namely the pronounced reduction in reverse yield stress and the transient change in hardening immediately after reversal. A purely isotropic hardening descriptor predicts only a symmetric expansion of the uniaxial yield stress with accumulated plastic strain, so it cannot recover this response. The discrepancy motivates constitutive descriptors based on kinematic translation, and in some materials additional distortional terms, rather than merely a larger or more flexible isotropic hardening law [ 10 ,  32 ,  38 ,  55 ,  57 ,  58 ]. Fig. 2 Schematic illustration of an observed Bauschinger response and the limitation of purely isotropic hardening in uniaxial tension–compression, in the spirit of [ 10 ,  32 ,  38 ,  48 ,  49 ]. Point 1 denotes the initial yield point; point 2 the maximum tensile deformation before unloading; point 3 the experimentally observed reverse yield stress in compression; and point 4 the reverse yield stress predicted by a purely isotropic hardening model. The vertical gap between points 3 and 4 denotes the reverse-yield overprediction error of the isotropic model, not an additional hardening increment

Although the idealised schematics suggest clean separations between constitutive descriptors, practical models often blur these distinctions. Translation of the locus can appear as directional softening in reverse loading; distortional laws almost always contain isotropic or kinematic components; and evolving anisotropy coefficients may mimic distortion when viewed through sparse experimental data. Table  3  should therefore be read as a  many-to-many map : rows correspond to dominant phenomena, but the descriptor and model-family columns identify typical, not unique, modelling routes [ 1 ,  10 ,  32 ,  38 ].

sections.heading: Microstructural mechanisms and internal variables
paragraphs: At the microstructural level, the observed phenomena in the first column of Table  3  arise from the interaction of several mechanisms, including dislocation storage and rearrangement, development and relaxation of internal back stresses, texture evolution, phase transformation and, in some cases, damage or void growth. The second column of Table  3  compresses these micromechanical effects into tractable constitutive descriptors. Simple isotropic hardening laws effectively lump the net effect of dislocation storage and other strengthening mechanisms into a single scalar internal variable. Kinematic hardening models introduce one or more backstress-like internal variables to represent the average directional bias in the microstructure, which is responsible for the Bauschinger effect and cyclic stabilisation. Distortional hardening formulations extend this idea further by introducing higher-order internal variables (e.g. fourth-order tensors or additional directional tensors) or by embedding directional dependencies directly in the yield function [ 10 ,  55 ,  57 ,  58 ].

Crystal-plasticity simulations and microstructural characterisation studies show that these mechanisms are often coupled: for example, dislocation structures that generate back stresses also affect the orientation distribution of slip systems and therefore the evolving anisotropy of the yield surface. Likewise, texture evolution under complex loading may produce directional hardening or softening that is not easily decomposed into purely isotropic and purely kinematic components [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ,  62 ]. In practice, phenomenological models make simplifying assumptions to achieve tractable descriptions: backstress variables are often related to averaged dislocation structures, while distortional components are constructed to match observed yield-locus evolutions under selected loading paths rather than to resolve the full microstructure.

From a modelling standpoint, the choice and number of internal variables reflect a compromise between physical transparency, numerical robustness and parameter identifiability. Models with few scalar and tensorial variables are easier to calibrate and implement but may lack the flexibility to reproduce strongly path-dependent behaviour. Models with richer internal variable sets can describe a wider range of phenomena but require extensive experimental data, careful regularisation and more elaborate stress-update algorithms [ 1 ,  63 ,  64 ].

sections.heading: Using the taxonomy for model selection
paragraphs: The structure of the table is consistent with the classifications proposed in [ 1 ,  7 ,  32 ], but it is organised here specifically for model selection and FE implementation purposes. The classification is not intended to be unique or exhaustive. Its practical value lies in making explicit that the same phenomenon may admit multiple modelling routes and that the choice between them depends on test availability, parameter identifiability, numerical robustness and the required predictive scope.

In the remainder of this paper, this taxonomy is used as an organising device. Section “ Phenomenological models for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening ” surveys representative phenomenological models and positions them within the rows of Table  3 , while emphasising where individual model families span more than one row because they combine several constitutive descriptors. Section “ Crystal-plasticity-based approaches and links to phenomenological models ” discusses how crystal-plasticity simulations can be employed to probe and refine this classification, particularly for materials and loading paths where experimental data are limited or difficult to obtain.

From an engineering viewpoint, Table  3  is meant to be read as a model- selection and test-design aid rather than as a purely conceptual summary. Given a target forming application and a limited budget of mechanical tests, the taxonomy indicates which observed deformation-induced hardening phenomena are likely to be critical, which constitutive ingredients are minimally required to represent them, and which tests increase or decrease the identifiability of the corresponding model parameters. In the next section, this taxonomy is used to organise representative phenomenological models, making explicit how their internal variables and evolution equations relate to the phenomena and descriptor classes summarised here.

sections.heading: Phenomenological models for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening
paragraphs: The taxonomy in Section “ Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families ” and Table  3  separates three layers that are often conflated in the literature: observed hardening phenomena, constitutive descriptor classes, and named model families. Phenomenological constitutive models can therefore be read as concrete implementations of one or more descriptor classes, targeted at selected rows of Table  3 . For practical FE applications, the central questions are not only which model is “most general”, but (i) which observed phenomena are critical for the target application, (ii) which constitutive ingredients are minimally required to reproduce them with acceptable numerical robustness and computational cost, and (iii) whether the available or affordable mechanical tests are sufficient to identify the corresponding parameter sets.

From this viewpoint, existing phenomenological models can be grouped into several broad families. The first family consists of anisotropic yield criteria combined with essentially isotropic hardening laws. Classical examples include Hill-type quadratic criteria and non-quadratic yield functions such as the Barlat family (e.g. Yld2000-2d, Yld2004-18p), coupled with Voce- or Hockett–Sherby-type isotropic hardening [ 4 ,  9 ,  23 ,  72 ,  73 ]. These models are primarily designed to capture planar anisotropy with expanding yield surfaces and correspond mainly to the first row in Table  3 . They are attractive for large-scale forming simulations because they involve a limited number of hardening parameters and can be calibrated from standard uniaxial and, optionally, plane-strain and equi-biaxial tests.

A second family augments anisotropic yield criteria with nonlinear kinematic hardening to represent Bauschinger effects and transient hardening/softening. Representative examples include Armstrong–Frederick and Chaboche-type models, as well as the widely used Yoshida–Uemori class and related anisotropic hardening formulations for sheet metals [ 38 ,  53 ,  54 ,  59 ]. These models primarily target the second and third rows in Table  3 , namely Bauschinger-type behaviour and transient responses under cyclic loading. They typically require tension–compression and cyclic tests for calibration and can significantly improve springback predictions compared to purely isotropic hardening, at the expense of additional internal variables and a more complex stress-update algorithm.

A third family introduces distortional or path-dependent hardening to capture yield-surface distortion and cross- or non-proportional hardening effects. Examples include the distortional yield surface models of François and co-workers, the directional distortion framework of Feigenbaum and Dafalias, and more recent high-anisotropic hardening (HAH/e-HAH) formulations that combine kinematic and distortional hardening within an anisotropic yield function [ 11 ,  12 ,  51 ,  52 ,  55 ,  56 ]. These models address the fourth and fifth rows in Table  3  and are particularly relevant for applications involving severe strain-path changes, non-proportional loading or complex forming histories. Their increased descriptive power comes with higher parameter density and more demanding identification requirements, typically involving multi-axial yield locus measurements and non-proportional loading paths.

Finally, a growing class of phenomenological descriptions explicitly targets the path-dependent evolution of  r -values and planar anisotropy, often by embedding evolving anisotropy parameters within advanced hardening frameworks or by interpolating between yield functions at different strain levels [ 54 ,  60 ,  61 ]. In many cases, crystal plasticity models are used as a virtual laboratory to generate synthetic yield loci and  r -value data, which are then used to inform and constrain the phenomenological model [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ]. These approaches correspond mainly to the last row in Table  3  and represent a bridge between purely macroscopic phenomenology and microstructure-based modelling.

In the remainder of this section, representative models from each family are reviewed with an emphasis on their mathematical structure, internal variables and evolution equations, and on the calibration data required to distinguish one model family from another. The aim is not to reproduce an exhaustive catalogue, but to identify a small set of constitutive archetypes, clarify the phenomena they can and cannot represent, and make the consequences for calibration and FE deployment explicit.

sections.heading: Anisotropic yield criteria for sheet metals
paragraphs: Classical criteria such as Hill’s quadratic model [ 69 ] and its extensions have been complemented by non-quadratic and, in some cases, non-associated yield functions, most notably the Barlat family of models [ 70 ,  71 ,  72 ,  73 – 74 ], in order to improve the description of planar anisotropy and yield loci in aluminium alloys and advanced high-strength steels [ 4 ,  7 ].

sections.heading: Quadratic Hill-type criteria
paragraphs: The main advantages of the Hill48 criterion are its simplicity, its linear association with a convex quadratic potential and the availability of closed-form expressions for the plastic strain-rate direction and the consistent elastoplastic tangent. These features make it attractive for large-scale FE simulations in automotive and packaging applications [ 7 ]. However, the quadratic shape limits its ability to match the yield loci of modern aluminium alloys and advanced steels, especially in shear and biaxial stress states, and it cannot represent tension–compression asymmetry. Furthermore, in the context of deformation-induced anisotropy, the Hill48 coefficients are often treated as constants; allowing them to evolve with plastic strain can partially account for distortional hardening but at the cost of additional parameters and potential identifiability issues [ 1 ]. Hill48 is therefore best regarded as a low-cost baseline criterion for row 1 of Table  3 : useful when monotonic planar anisotropy matters, but not a substitute for missing kinematic or distortional hardening.

sections.heading: Non-quadratic and Barlat-type yield functions
paragraphs: To overcome the limitations of quadratic criteria, a family of non-quadratic, often homogeneous polynomial yield functions has been developed, notably by Barlat and co-workers [ 70 ,  71 ,  72 ,  73 ,  74 – 75 ]. These models introduce anisotropy through linear or nonlinear transformations of the stress tensor, followed by a non-quadratic equivalent stress measure defined in terms of the principal values of the transformed stress [ 76 ,  77 – 78 ]. Typical examples include the Yld1991, Yld2000-2d and Yld2004-18p criteria, which are now standard tools in sheet-forming simulations [ 4 ,  7 ].

From an FE implementation standpoint, non-quadratic yield functions introduce several additional challenges. The equivalent stress measure is often defined implicitly in terms of principal values, requiring eigenvalue decompositions or iterative procedures to evaluate the yield function and its derivatives. The consistent tangent operator becomes more involved, particularly when the yield function is non-smooth or has kinks in certain directions. Efficient and robust stress-update algorithms therefore rely on careful numerical treatment of the principal values and their derivatives, as well as regularisation strategies to avoid loss of convergence in regions where the yield locus has reduced curvature [ 64 ]. Despite these complexities, Barlat-type criteria now form the de facto standard for modelling planar anisotropy in many industrial sheet-forming applications [ 1 ,  7 ]. Their practical value is highest when the engineering question is the fidelity of the initial or weakly evolved yield locus under plane stress; they cannot compensate for a hardening law that lacks the internal variables required by the loading history.

A useful way to interpret the choice between Hill-type and Barlat-type criteria is therefore not “simple versus advanced” in the abstract, but “sufficient versus insufficient for the stress states that matter”. If monotonic uniaxial and near-plane-strain states dominate and calibration resources are limited, a quadratic criterion may remain adequate. If balanced biaxial, shear and directional  r -value accuracy are central, non-quadratic criteria are usually warranted. In either case, the yield criterion should be selected together with the hardening law rather than as an isolated front-end fitting exercise.

sections.heading: Isotropic, kinematic and distortional hardening laws
paragraphs: Within Eq.  1 , hardening laws determine how the size, position and shape of the yield locus evolve. In the taxonomy of Section “ Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families ”, isotropic hardening governs uniform expansion, kinematic hardening governs translation, and distortional hardening governs shape changes of the yield locus. In phenomenological models for sheet metals, these components are often combined, either explicitly through separate internal variables or implicitly through evolution laws for anisotropy parameters in the yield criterion [ 1 ,  10 ,  38 ,  55 ,  57 ,  58 ]. The key engineering issue is therefore structural adequacy: a model should be judged first by whether its internal variables can reproduce the phenomena that control the application, and only then by how well its parameters fit a particular subset of experiments.

sections.heading: Isotropic hardening
paragraphs: Purely isotropic hardening can provide adequate predictions for forming operations dominated by monotonic loading with limited strain-path changes. However, as illustrated in Fig.  2 , it fails to capture the Bauschinger effect and the pronounced softening often observed in reverse loading. In terms of the taxonomy in Table  3 , isotropic hardening alone cannot represent kinematic or distortional effects; at best it can mimic some aspects of mixed hardening through carefully chosen scalar laws, but only for a restricted set of loading paths [ 1 ,  10 ,  32 ]. Accordingly, scalar hardening should be seen as sufficient only when the application is genuinely dominated by monotonic expansion of the yield locus. Once reverse loading, springback or non-proportional path changes matter, improving the scalar fit in Eqs.  5 – 7  cannot repair the missing physics.

sections.heading: Kinematic hardening and combined models
paragraphs: In practice, kinematic hardening models are rarely used in isolation. Most engineering implementations combine an isotropic component, which governs the overall expansion of the yield locus, with a kinematic component, which accounts for translation and partial memory of the loading history. The number and type of backstress variables reflect a trade-off between flexibility and identifiability: multiple backstresses can reproduce complex cyclic responses but require extensive reverse and cyclic test data for reliable calibration [ 1 ,  10 ,  25 ]. Yoshida–Uemori-type models can be viewed as two-surface realisations of this idea, in which a translating current yield surface evolves inside a bounding surface so that transient hardening/softening and saturation under reverse loading are represented more sharply than in a single-backstress law [ 38 ,  54 ]. From a numerical viewpoint, nonlinear kinematic hardening laws often introduce additional stiffness in the local stress-update problem; robust return-mapping algorithms and consistent tangents are essential to maintain global convergence in FE simulations [ 64 ]. The main limitation is therefore not conceptual reach but identifiability: a seemingly excellent fit to one tension–compression data set does not imply that the calibrated backstresses are unique or transferable to a different strain-path history.

sections.heading: Distortional hardening and evolving anisotropy parameters
paragraphs: Foundational theories by Rees [ 90 ] and Ortiz and Popov [ 91 ] established the thermodynamics of distortional hardening. More recently, Manopulo et al. [ 92 ,  93 ] have proposed models specifically addressing the transition from isotropic to distortional hardening. Examples include the microstructurally-motivated models of Teodosiu and Hu [ 60 ,  94 ], the yield-surface-distortion models of François [ 55 ], the finite-deformation distortional framework of Pietryga, Vladimirov and Reese [ 95 ], and the Homogeneous Anisotropic Hardening (HAH) approaches introduced by Barlat and co-workers and later extended in plane stress [ 52 ,  65 ,  96 ,  97 – 98 ], which employ a fluctuating stress field to capture Bauschinger-like and directional hardening responses without introducing a conventional physical backstress. More recent frameworks by Shen, Lattanzi and co-workers [ 57 ,  58 ] explicitly allow the anisotropy parameters themselves to evolve with loading history.

From an FE perspective, distortional models are more demanding than purely isotropic or isotropic–kinematic formulations. The yield locus may become strongly non-symmetric and exhibit regions of low curvature or near-corners, which can impair the performance of standard return-mapping schemes [ 64 ]. Moreover, the evolution laws for anisotropy parameters may depend on the full loading history, making the stress update problem more path-dependent. These issues motivate the use of crystal-plasticity simulations and tailored experimental programmes to guide the construction and calibration of distortional hardening models [ 1 ,  19 ,  20 ]. The key gain is clear: rows 4–6 of Table  3  cannot be reproduced convincingly without some mechanism of this kind. The key price is equally clear: parameter density, derivative complexity and identifiability all increase sharply.

sections.heading: Model capabilities in the taxonomy framework

paragraphs: The phenomenological models reviewed above can now be assessed in terms of their ability to represent the hardening classes identified in Table  3  and the experimental signatures summarised in Table  2 . A useful reviewer-level criterion is structural adequacy: if the application demands a phenomenon that the model class cannot generate, no amount of parameter optimisation will compensate for that mismatch. Conversely, if the process is genuinely monotonic, a highly parameterised path-dependent model may create more calibration and implementation risk than value.

From a practical viewpoint, Tables  4  and  5  are more useful when read as an elimination procedure than as an invitation to always choose the richest model. If the target application never experiences meaningful reverse loading, a kinematic or distortional law is an unnecessary calibration and implementation burden. If bend–unbend or cyclic path changes dominate, however, then a scalar law is structurally inadequate regardless of how well it fits monotonic tensile data. Similarly, if path-dependent  r -values or evolving biaxial loci are central, the burden of an evolving-anisotropy or CP-informed route is justified; if not, it may simply add non-identifiable parameters. This “fit only what the application can reveal” principle is central for Q1-level engineering review work because many apparent disagreements between model families are in fact mismatches between the data collected and the phenomena that must be reproduced.

sections.heading: Illustrative application cases
paragraphs: As an illustration, consider first an automotive component manufactured from a dual-phase or advanced high-strength steel, such as DP780 or DP980. For accurate prediction of springback in channel bending, hat-shape or roll-forming processes, it is well established that both Bauschinger effects and transient hardening/softening under reverse loading are critical [ 38 ,  54 ,  100 ,  101 ,  102 – 103 ]. In the terminology of Table  3 , this corresponds primarily to rows 1–3 and often also to row 4 when yield-surface distortion is significant. Tables  4  and  5  then indicate that an anisotropic yield function (e.g. Hill’48 or Yld2000-2d) combined with nonlinear kinematic hardening of Yoshida–Uemori or Chaboche type, and possibly augmented by distortional hardening, is a minimally adequate choice. The same tables also make explicit that such a choice implies a moderate-to-high parameter density and requires tension–compression and cyclic tests, in addition to multi-directional uniaxial and bulge tests, for reliable calibration and validation of springback predictions [ 38 ,  54 ,  101 ,  102 ].

As a second example, consider aluminium alloy sheets of the AA5xxx or AA6xxx series used for outer body panels. Here, planar anisotropy and the evolution of  r -values with strain and strain path are often of comparable importance to springback, and experimental studies have shown significant sensitivity of springback to the combination of anisotropic yield function and kinematic hardening, especially when the Bauschinger effect is pronounced [ 104 ,  105 ]. In the taxonomy of Table  3 , rows 1 and 6 (planar anisotropy and path-dependent anisotropy evolution) are therefore key, with possible contributions from rows 2 and 3 for Bauschinger and transient effects. Tables  4  and  5  indicate that model families with evolving anisotropy parameters or interpolation between yield functions, potentially informed by crystal-plasticity-based virtual laboratories, are natural candidates for such materials. The tables also make explicit that the corresponding calibration effort is higher, typically requiring multi-directional uniaxial tests at several strain levels, and that CP or CPFE simulations can help reduce experimental demands by supplying synthetic yield loci and  r -value data [ 104 ,  105 – 106 ,  110 ,  117 ].

sections.heading: Crystal-plasticity-based approaches and links to phenomenological models
paragraphs: Crystal plasticity (CP) frameworks provide a microstructure-sensitive description of anisotropic plastic flow by resolving slip activity, lattice rotation and hardening at the crystal scale. Relative to the phenomenological models reviewed in Sections “ Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families ” and “ Phenomenological models for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening ”, CP has three distinct roles in the present review. First, it offers a mechanistic interpretation of the phenomena in Table  3 . Second, it can generate transferable observables under loading paths that are sparse, expensive or difficult to realise experimentally. Third, it can be used to test whether a candidate phenomenological model family is structurally adequate before that model is deployed in large-scale forming simulations [ 19 ,  20 ,  62 ,  112 ,  117 ]. The crucial caveat is that CP predictions are conditional rather than absolute: they depend on texture statistics, phase topology, boundary conditions, slip-system constitutive choices and numerical resolution. Accordingly, CP-derived data should be treated as model-informed constraints for phenomenology, not as unconditional ground truth.

sections.heading: Role of crystal plasticity in modelling deformation-induced anisotropy
paragraphs: By construction, CP resolves the main microstructural sources of deformation-induced anisotropy: initial and evolving texture, phase morphology, grain interactions, latent hardening and lattice rotation. It is therefore well suited to explain why the macroscopic observables in Table  3  change under path reversals, cross loading, plane-strain loading or multi-step forming routes. In nominally rate-independent applications, many practical CP implementations still rely on a small viscoplastic regularisation or analogous numerical device. This matters in review terms because predicted reverse-loading transients and path-change responses depend not only on texture evolution, but also on the chosen slip-rate law and hardening architecture.

From the viewpoint of the present manuscript, CP is therefore not a routine replacement for phenomenological sheet-metal models. Its value is highest when the target response is strongly path dependent, when microstructure-sensitive materials are under consideration, or when the required experiments are too sparse to discriminate reliably between competing phenomenological architectures [ 19 ,  20 ,  109 ,  112 ].

sections.heading: Representative CP frameworks and numerical realisations
paragraphs: CP models for engineering sheet materials are implemented in three broad numerical settings. Mean-field schemes, such as Taylor-type and viscoplastic self-consistent (VPSC) approaches, represent the polycrystal through homogenised grain interactions. They are comparatively efficient and are often sufficient for trend studies, first-pass parameter identification and the prediction of directional stresses,  r -values and texture evolution under simple or moderately complex loading paths [ 19 ,  20 ,  99 ]. Full-field CPFE models resolve grain-scale heterogeneity explicitly and are therefore better suited to localisation-sensitive studies, multi-phase microstructures and cases where local strain/stress distributions matter for the interpretation of macroscopic anisotropy or failure precursors [ 19 ,  62 ,  109 ].

Between these two extremes, spectral or FFT-based CP solvers provide a useful intermediate route for virtual-test campaigns on periodic RVEs. Such frameworks retain full-field heterogeneity but can be markedly more efficient than classical CPFE for repeated yield-surface evaluations, sensitivity studies or evolving-yield-function updates [ 107 ,  108 ]. From the perspective of the present review, this numerical hierarchy is important because it determines what kind of CP evidence is realistically available to inform phenomenological calibration. A mean-field model may be sufficient to rank competing yield criteria, whereas full-field CPFE or spectral solvers become more attractive when yield loci must be generated at several strain levels or under path changes.

Direct component-scale forming simulations with CP as the primary constitutive description remain exceptional in industrial practice because of cost, parameter-identification effort and the need for detailed microstructural input. Consequently, the most plausible engineering role of CP is usually indirect: to interpret experiments, to screen model families and to generate selected synthetic data for macroscopic model development.

sections.heading: Crystal plasticity as a virtual laboratory: workflow and transferable observables
paragraphs: The useful output of a CP campaign is usually not the CP model itself, but a curated set of transferable macroscopic observables. A disciplined CP-based virtual-laboratory workflow for sheet metals can therefore be organised into five stages:  Microstructure characterisation and RVE construction.  Establish the texture, phase fractions, grain-size statistics and morphology that define the material state to be represented. CP parameter identification.  Calibrate the slip-system constitutive parameters against a baseline experimental set so that the CP model reproduces the essential monotonic responses of the actual material state. Virtual testing.  Subject the calibrated RVE or CPFE model to targeted loading paths that are discriminating for the phenomenological problem of interest: multi- directional tension, plane-strain states, equi-biaxial loading, reverse loading or non-proportional paths. Observable extraction.  Reduce the virtual-test output to macroscopic quantities that can actually be transferred: directional yield stresses,  r -values, yield-locus points at prescribed plastic work, reverse-loading metrics and sensitivity trends with respect to texture or phase topology. Phenomenological calibration and validation.  Use these observables, together with a reserved set of physical experiments, to calibrate and then test the phenomenological model out of sample. This last stage is essential. If all physical data are consumed in calibrating the CP model and all phenomenological data are then generated synthetically from that same model, the macroscopic law is merely inheriting the CP model-form error in a hidden way. For that reason, the most credible virtual-laboratory studies use experiments to anchor the CP model, use CP to fill selected gaps, and retain at least some independent experiments for validation [ 110 ,  112 ,  117 ].

The main macro–micro transfer routes, their intended phenomenological use, and the associated caveats are summarised in Table  6 . Table 6 Typical transfer map from CP virtual-laboratory outputs to phenomenological modelling choices and calibration targets. The key point is that CP outputs usually constrain model structure and parameter ranges; they rarely translate into one-to-one macroscopic parameters CP-derived output Use in phenomenology Main transfer caveat Directional uniaxial yield stresses and  r -values Calibration of the initial anisotropic yield function and baseline directional hardening trends Strongly influenced by the assumed texture statistics and by how macroscopic averaging is performed; they do not by themselves identify path-dependent hardening. Plane-strain and equi-biaxial yield points; selected locus segments Discrimination between simple Hill-type forms and advanced non-quadratic yield criteria Sensitive to RVE size, boundary conditions and the convention used to define first yield or offset yield in the virtual test. Yield loci evolved to fixed plastic work or strain levels Evidence for whether evolving anisotropy or distortional hardening is structurally required Dense virtual data can hide correlation and identifiability problems; a high-parameter macromodel may simply absorb CP model bias. Reverse-loading curves and transient hardening after path changes Screening of backstress, two-surface or distortional-hardening architectures Reverse responses are not uniquely mapped to one macroscopic internal-variable set; slip-system hardening choices and rate regularisation also affect the result. Sensitivity to texture, phase fraction and grain morphology Model-family ranking, experimental-test prioritisation and robustness studies Useful mainly for trends and comparative sensitivity; rarely a direct route to unique parameter values. The workflow above is most useful for the taxonomy rows associated with Bauschinger response, transient hardening, yield-locus distortion, cross-hardening and path-dependent anisotropy (rows 2–6 in Table  3 ), namely the situations in which simple proportional- loading calibration data are least informative.

sections.heading: Macro–micro transfer, uncertainty and identifiability
paragraphs: The bridge from CP to phenomenology is useful, but it is never automatic. The first source of uncertainty lies in the microstructure representation itself: texture truncation, RVE size, phase-topology reconstruction and boundary conditions can all shift the predicted macroscopic response, especially in multi-phase steels and strongly textured sheets. The second source is constitutive model form at the crystal scale: slip families, latent hardening, backstress architecture, rate sensitivity, twinning or transformation mechanisms and their calibration all affect the virtual output. The third source is numerical: spatial resolution, periodicity assumptions and yield-extraction conventions can change the apparent anisotropy or reverse- loading response [ 19 ,  20 ,  107 ,  108 ,  112 ].

A further and frequently underemphasised point is that more virtual data are not equivalent to more independent information. Yield-locus points generated from the same calibrated CP model are correlated; so are directional responses extracted from the same underlying texture representation. Consequently, fitting a high-parameter phenomenological law to a dense CP data cloud can mask rather than resolve identifiability problems. In review terms, CP is therefore most valuable as a structural discriminator—for example, to decide whether fixed anisotropy, combined hardening or an evolving-anisotropy architecture is warranted—before it is used as a high-volume data generator [ 99 ,  107 ,  117 ].

The safest transfer route is therefore a hybrid one. Experiments should anchor the baseline stress–strain response, at least part of the directional anisotropy, and ideally one path- change or biaxial benchmark of direct engineering relevance. CP can then be used to interpolate between scarce experiments, to generate candidate loci at intermediate strain levels, or to probe sensitivities that would be prohibitively expensive to map experimentally [ 110 ,  111 – 112 ]. Used in this way, CP reduces experimental burden without pretending to abolish it.

sections.heading: When is CP assistance justified in practice?
paragraphs: For engineering sheet plasticity, a CP-assisted route is most strongly justified when one or more of the following conditions hold: the application is sensitive to evolving anisotropy, reverse loading or springback, so that monotonic proportional tests are insufficient; the material is strongly texture sensitive or microstructure sensitive, as in many aluminium alloys, multiphase AHSS or other heterogeneous sheet systems; the phenomenological model under consideration has too many competing structures to be discriminated reliably by the available physical tests alone; or the missing loading states are experimentally difficult, costly or poorly repeatable, but sufficient microstructural information exists to make CP predictions credible. By contrast, CP assistance is often of limited marginal value when the target application is dominated by monotonic proportional loading, when a fixed-anisotropy model already reproduces the required observables within engineering tolerance, or when microstructural characterisation is too uncertain for the virtual tests to be trusted. In such cases, the additional modelling burden may exceed the gain in predictive capability.

In summary, crystal-plasticity-based approaches are best viewed as an intermediate layer between microstructure and macroscopic phenomenology. Their main engineering value is not to replace the macromodel in routine FE forming simulations, but to explain when advanced hardening structures are needed, to provide selected synthetic observables where experiments are sparse, and to bound the plausible calibration space of phenomenological models. CP-based ductile damage and fracture modelling fall outside the scope of the present review and are therefore not treated explicitly.

sections.heading: Computational aspects for FE implementation
paragraphs: The engineering usefulness of anisotropic hardening models is decided as much by the  local constitutive update  as by the constitutive equations themselves. A model family may be structurally capable of reproducing Bauschinger effects, cross-hardening or yield-surface rotation, yet still perform poorly in finite element (FE) simulations if the local stress update, algorithmic tangent or parameter-identification workflow is fragile. For the sheet-forming applications targeted in this review, the practical computational questions are therefore fairly specific: how the constitutive update is written, how plane stress and large rotations are handled, how local and global Newton iterations are coupled, and how a parameter set is identified without confusing numerical artefacts with constitutive shortcomings.

The aim of this section is not to reproduce full derivations from standard computational plasticity texts [ 26 ,  113 ], but to make explicit the minimal algorithmic structure required for deploying the model classes discussed in Section “ Phenomenological models for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening ”. The discussion is organised around four practical layers: the generic local constitutive problem, the distinction between rate-independent and rate-dependent integration, the kinematic issues introduced by plane stress and finite strains, and the local/global numerical safeguards needed for robust industrial FE calculations. Two identification templates are then restated in a form that is directly compatible with the local integration structure.

sections.heading: Generic local constitutive update: rate-independent setting
Algorithm 1. Generic fully implicit local update for anisotropic hardening models
Rate-dependent or numerically regularised integration
paragraphs: This distinction matters because numerical regularisation can improve robustness while quietly altering the constitutive response. The temptation is obvious: a small viscosity often suppresses switching chatter and can stabilise highly coupled distortional models or non-associated flow rules. But a regularisation that is too strong may broaden yield transitions, alter hysteresis-loop shape and blur the very path-dependence one is trying to model. Recent implementation papers on anisotropic distortional hardening illustrate both sides of this trade-off: fully implicit coupled solvers can be made robust, but they often require careful residual scaling, while user-friendly finite-difference-based derivatives reduce coding effort at the price of step-size sensitivity that must be checked explicitly [ 56 ,  115 ,  116 ]. A production FE model should therefore report whether rate dependence is material or algorithmic, and should document the corresponding sensitivity study.

sections.heading: Plane stress, objective rates and finite-strain transfer between codes
paragraphs: At larger strains the kinematic framework adds another layer of non-equivalence. Small-strain hypo-elastic updates with Jaumann-type rates may be adequate for algorithm development or limited benchmarking, but they can produce spurious shear stresses or artificial anisotropy under large rotations. Finite-strain frameworks based on the multiplicative decomposition of the deformation gradient, or on logarithmic stress/strain measures, provide a more robust basis for large sheet-forming deformations [ 26 ,  113 ]. When constitutive models are transferred between different FE environments (for example, between shell and solid formulations, or between user subroutines with different stress/strain measures), the transfer should be treated as a constitutive reimplementation rather than a mere syntax conversion. The stress measure, work conjugacy, pull-back/push-forward operations and objective rate assumptions must all be documented explicitly.

sections.heading: Algorithmic tangents and local/global convergence
Frequent numerical failure modes and practical remedies
Template A: purely macroscopic identification and FE deployment
paragraphs: Template A is appropriate when the experimental programme is rich enough to identify the chosen phenomenological model without recourse to a microstructure-resolved virtual laboratory. The key point is to separate constitutive adequacy from identifiability. A model should first be chosen because it is  structurally capable  of reproducing the observed hardening signatures in Tables  3  and  5 ; only then should its parameters be fitted.

A robust macroscopic workflow can be organised as follows:  Model-family selection.  Choose the simplest model family that is structurally adequate for the observed behaviour: monotonic anisotropy, reverse loading, cross- hardening or distortional evolution. Avoid introducing internal variables whose signatures are not supported by the available tests. Staged identification.  Calibrate elastic constants and initial anisotropy from monotonic tests first; identify scalar hardening next; then determine kinematic and, if justified, distortional variables from reverse or non-proportional tests. This staged order reduces parameter compensation. Material-point verification.  Implement the local update and consistent tangent, then verify proportional, reverse and orthogonal loading paths in a single integration point or single-element setting before any component simulation is attempted. If an analytical tangent is coded, compare it against numerical differentiation during development. Inverse identification.  Define a weighted objective function using the observables that motivated the model choice in the first place: directional yield stresses,  r -values, reverse-yield stresses, Bauschinger ratios, loop shape and, where available, yield-locus evolution at multiple pre-strains. Component-level validation and deployment.  Validate the calibrated model on benchmark components such as U-bend, draw-bend or hat-channel tests before transferring it to full industrial process simulations. This template underlies many successful springback studies in AHSS and aluminium sheets based on anisotropic yield criteria coupled to Yoshida–Uemori or Chaboche-type hardening [ 38 ,  54 ,  101 ,  102 ,  114 ]. Its main limitation is not computational feasibility but parameter identifiability once the model family becomes too flexible for the available test matrix.

sections.heading: Template B: CP-assisted identification with virtual-laboratory constraints
paragraphs: Template B is intended for the opposite situation: the phenomenological model is structurally reasonable, but the physical laboratory alone does not constrain all of its parameters well enough for robust extrapolation. In that case the CP virtual laboratory discussed in Section “ Crystal plasticity as a virtual laboratory: workflow and transferable observables ” is used as a  supporting  source of information, not as a replacement for experiments.

A practical CP-assisted workflow is:  Baseline phenomenological calibration.  Execute Template A to identify the parameters that are already well constrained by experiments. Calibration of the CP virtual laboratory.  Calibrate the CP model so that it reproduces the key macroscopic responses that are already trusted experimentally, including flow curves, selected yield loci and  r -values. Generation of targeted virtual data.  Use the CP virtual laboratory only for the loading paths that are experimentally missing or prohibitively expensive, such as non-proportional path changes, additional pre-strain states or microstructure-sensitive yield-locus evolution. Augmented inverse identification.  Add these targeted virtual observables to the objective function with explicit weighting. Experimental data should remain the anchor; synthetic data should regularise underconstrained directions in parameter space rather than dominate the fit. Independent validation.  Validate the resulting phenomenological model on component-level tests and, where useful, against selected CPFE simulations. Persistent disagreement should trigger either a redesign of the test matrix or a reduction of the phenomenological model freedom. Used in this restrained way, CP assistance can convert an underdetermined phenomenological fit into a reproducible identification problem without forcing full CPFE into routine industrial analyses [ 110 ,  111 – 112 ,  117 ]. The main danger is methodological overreach: if synthetic data overwhelm the physical test anchor, one may obtain a model that reproduces the virtual laboratory better than the material itself.

sections.heading: Verification ladder and industrial deployment
paragraphs: Before any advanced anisotropic hardening model is trusted in production FE calculations, a verification ladder should be completed explicitly:  Material-point tests.  Check monotonic, reverse and non-proportional loading paths; verify local convergence, dissipation and tolerance sensitivity. Element/formulation tests.  Compare shell and solid responses where possible, verify plane-stress enforcement, and assess sensitivity to element type, time step and integration scheme. Benchmark components.  Reproduce standard springback/forming benchmarks before attempting large industrial models with complex contact and process history. Production governance.  Record the constitutive version, solver tolerances, substepping rules, line-search strategy, tangent type and calibration data set together with the fitted parameter vector. Otherwise, later discrepancies are impossible to diagnose cleanly. The practical conclusion is blunt. The failure of an FE prediction should not be attributed to the constitutive model alone until the local update, the tangent, the plane-stress handling and the identification workflow have all been verified. For deformation-induced anisotropic hardening in sheet metals, constitutive choice and numerical implementation are inseparable parts of the same engineering model.

sections.heading: Synthesis: engineering takeaways, persistent debates and research priorities
paragraphs: The review can be reduced to one practical message: model selection for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening should be driven by  structural adequacy ,  available characterisation data  and  implementation budget  at the same time. A model is not preferable because it is more elaborate in the abstract; it is preferable only when the target application exhibits loading-path effects that the simpler model cannot represent and when the available calibration data can actually constrain the added freedom.

sections.heading: Engineering takeaways for model selection
(i) Structural adequacy matters more than nominal generality
paragraphs: For applications dominated by monotonic or only mildly path-changing loading, anisotropic yield criteria combined with isotropic hardening remain a defensible baseline because they are lean, identifiable and numerically robust. Once reverse loading, transient Bauschinger response, cross-hardening or pronounced yield-locus distortion become design-relevant, however, that baseline ceases to be structurally adequate and one must move toward nonlinear kinematic, distortional or evolving-anisotropy formulations. The key decision is therefore not “simple versus advanced” in the abstract, but “adequate versus inadequate for the path history that actually governs the component”.

sections.heading: (ii) Calibration data must match the phenomena the model is supposed to reproduce
paragraphs: The taxonomy developed in Section “ Taxonomy linking observed phenomena, constitutive evolution modes and model families ” and the decision tables in Sections “ Phenomenological models for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening ”–“ Computational aspects for FE implementation ” imply a direct rule: do not select a model family whose signature mechanisms cannot be constrained by the available test matrix. Directional uniaxial tests are informative for initial anisotropy and hardening level, but they do not identify reverse re-yielding, transient stagnation, cross-hardening or distortion by themselves. If those effects matter for springback or localisation, the test programme must be expanded accordingly; otherwise the additional constitutive freedom is largely nominal and may degrade robustness rather than improve prediction.

sections.heading: (iii) Crystal plasticity is most valuable as a constrained support tool
paragraphs: Crystal plasticity contributes most when it is used to interpret mechanisms, generate targeted synthetic observables for missing loading paths, and regularise underdetermined phenomenological fits. It is far less attractive when treated as a default replacement for phenomenological models in large industrial FE campaigns. For engineering workflow design, the productive question is thus not whether CP is “more physical” in general, but whether it reduces uncertainty in a way that justifies its calibration and computational cost for the material system at hand.

sections.heading: Persistent modelling debates
(i) Complexity versus robustness
paragraphs: This trade-off remains central. Rich distortional or evolving-anisotropy frameworks can reproduce more of the experimentally observed phenomenology, but they also increase parameter density, identifiability difficulty and the risk of local-update or global-convergence problems. Leaner models often extrapolate more honestly when the test basis is limited. In practice, the best model for a Q1-level engineering application is usually the simplest formulation that remains structurally adequate for the target path changes and stress states.

sections.heading: (ii) Associated versus non-associated descriptions
paragraphs: There is still no universally superior choice. Non-associated formulations can fit certain stress and strain-ratio data more flexibly, especially when yield and flow characteristics decouple, but that flexibility comes at a cost in tangent construction, algorithm design and parameter identification. Associated formulations remain attractive because they are easier to deploy and to verify, even when they cannot capture every directional nuance of the plastic flow.

sections.heading: (iii) Constitutive choice and numerical implementation cannot be separated
paragraphs: A recurring mistake in the literature is to discuss model form and FE implementation as if they were independent layers. They are not. A model with elegant phenomenology but poorly conditioned local residuals, fragile plane-stress enforcement or inconsistent tangents is not an engineering solution. Conversely, apparently modest constitutive forms can perform very well when the local update, calibration workflow and verification ladder are designed carefully.

sections.heading: Research priorities
paragraphs: The most consequential next steps are now fairly clear:  Benchmark-quality path-change data.  Public, well-documented data sets for reverse, cyclic and non-proportional loading in industrially relevant sheets are needed to support fair comparison between model classes. Identifiability and uncertainty analysis.  Model selection should be coupled to sensitivity analysis, parameter identifiability and uncertainty propagation rather than treated as a purely descriptive fitting exercise. Reduced-order CP-assisted calibration.  The most promising CP route is not brute-force replacement of phenomenology, but targeted transfer of microstructure-informed observables into leaner macroscopic models. Open implementations and verification ladders.  Reproducible material-point tests, benchmark FE problems and openly inspectable implementations would do more for the field than yet another under-documented parameter set. Coupled anisotropy–rate–damage frameworks.  Future constitutive developments should address the interaction of evolving anisotropy with rate sensitivity, unloading and damage/fracture without sacrificing numerical tractability.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Deformation-induced anisotropic hardening in metallic sheet materials is not a marginal correction to classical plasticity; it is often the mechanism that separates acceptable springback and localisation predictions from unusable ones. The difficulty is not merely phenomenological. The relevant effects are path-dependent, partly overlapping, and unequally visible across different test types, which means that constitutive modelling, parameter identification and FE implementation must be planned together.

The central contribution of this review has therefore been to recast the subject into an engineering decision framework. Experimentally observed responses were separated from constitutive evolution descriptors and from representative model families, so that the choice of model can be tied directly to observable hardening signatures and to minimum characterisation requirements. This structure clarifies why monotonic directional data may be sufficient for some applications, yet grossly insufficient for others involving reversal, transient behaviour or yield-locus distortion.

A second conclusion is methodological. The best constitutive model is rarely the most elaborate one available; it is the simplest model that remains structurally adequate for the loading paths, stress states and decision variables that matter in the target simulation. Reverse-loading, cyclic and non-proportional tests should therefore be viewed not as optional refinements but as selection tools that determine whether kinematic, distortional or evolving-anisotropy ingredients are genuinely warranted. Crystal plasticity is most useful in the same spirit: as a virtual laboratory that supplements and constrains macroscopic calibration, not as a routine substitute for phenomenological modelling in large industrial FE analyses.

A third conclusion concerns computation. For the class of models reviewed here, numerical credibility depends as much on the local constitutive update, plane-stress enforcement, tangent construction and verification ladder as on the symbolic form of the hardening law itself. A model that fits laboratory data but fails under robust FE deployment is not yet an engineering model. This is why Section “ Computational aspects for FE implementation ” treated implementation structure, failure modes and identification workflow as first-order content rather than as afterthoughts.

Relative to prior reviews, the present manuscript is intended to contribute a more operational bridge between experiments, model-family selection, CP-assisted calibration and FE deployment. Its scope has nonetheless remained deliberately limited to deformation-induced anisotropic hardening and closely related constitutive issues; damage, ductile fracture and forming-limit methodologies were discussed only where they affect the interpretation or deployment of hardening models. Within that scope, the main recommendation is straightforward: choose the leanest model that is structurally adequate, calibrate it against the phenomena that actually matter, and do not separate constitutive ambition from numerical verification.
