Multi-axial yield-locus measurements after different pre-strain levels (uniaxial, plane strain, equi-biaxial); tension–compression and two-step non-proportional loading paths to trigger distortion and validate the evolution of shape in the deviatoric plane [ 11 ,  12 ,  51 ,  55 ,  56 ]
Cross-hardening and non-proportional hardening under orthogonal or multi-step loading
Path-dependent directional hardening, structure-tensor effects and sometimes non-coaxial or higher-order internal variables

Models with direction-dependent or path-dependent hardening internal variables (e.g. Teodosiu–Hu class, HAH-type models with non-proportional loading terms, enhanced kinematic/distortional formulations with additional structure tensors) [ 1 ,  51 ,  60 ,  97 ,  98 ]

Two- and three-step loading paths with cross-loading or orthogonal reloading (e.g. tension in RD followed by tension or shear in TD); combined with yield-locus measurements to expose cross-hardening and non-proportional hardening effects [ 50 ,  60 ]
Path-dependent evolution of  r -values and planar anisotropy
Explicit evolution of anisotropy coefficients or interpolated yield surfaces; mixed hardening linked to texture and loading-path history

Mixed kinematic/distortional hardening within anisotropic yield functions, sometimes augmented by interpolation schemes between yield functions at different strain levels (e.g. Yoshida-type interpolation, path-dependent anisotropic hardening); CP-informed phenomenological models with evolving anisotropy parameters [ 20 ,  54 ,  57 ,  58 ,  61 ]

Uniaxial tests in multiple in-plane directions at several strain levels (including after strain-path changes); complementary CP or CPFE simulations used as a virtual laboratory to generate synthetic  r -value data for calibration when experiments are limited

tables.caption: Decision-oriented overview of representative phenomenological model archetypes for deformation-induced anisotropic hardening in sheet metals. “Rows” refers to the targeted hardening classes in Table  3
headers: Typical failure mode if used beyond scope
rows: Hill48 + scalar hardening [ 69 ]
Fixed quadratic anisotropy + one scalar hardening law (e.g. Voce / Swift)
Mainly row 1
Good monotonic fit but poor reverse-loading and shear/biaxial fidelity; springback errors are then blamed on parameters rather than on missing mechanisms.
Barlat-type yield function + scalar hardening [ 70 ,  72 ,  73 ]
Non-quadratic anisotropic equivalent stress + one scalar hardening law
Mainly row 1; partial support for row 6 at small strains
Multi-direction uniaxial data,  r -values, and at least limited biaxial / plane-strain information
Excellent monotonic yield-locus description can mask the absence of Bauschinger and distortional physics under path changes.
Yield criterion + Chaboche / Yoshida–Uemori-type hardening [ 10 ,  38 ,  54 ]
Fixed anisotropy + isotropic hardening + one or more backstresses or two-surface structure
Rows 1–3
Multi-direction uniaxial tests plus tension–compression or cyclic tests at several pre-strains
Backstress parameters may be non-unique if only one reverse-loading path is used; performance degrades when strong distortion or evolving anisotropy dominates.
Distortional / HAH / directional hardening models [ 11 ,  52 ,  55 ,  65 ,  96 ,  98 ]
Fixed or evolving anisotropic yield function + dedicated distortional variables, fluctuating stress, or directional hardening terms
Rows 1 and 4–5
Multi-axial yield loci at several pre-strains; non-proportional cross-loading tests; ideally shear and biaxial reloadings
Parameter density rises quickly; without rich path-change data the model can fit one distortion scenario while failing on another.
Evolving-anisotropy / CP-informed phenomenology [ 19 ,  57 ,  58 ]
History-dependent anisotropy parameters, yield-function interpolation, or phenomenological laws constrained by CP data
Rows 1 and 6, with possible overlap into rows 4–5
Multi-direction tests at several strain levels, often supplemented by CP virtual tests for loci and  r -values
Calibration becomes a coupled modelling problem; if the CP or interpolation basis is weak, apparent sophistication can hide poor transferability.

tables.caption: Typical transfer map from CP virtual-laboratory outputs to phenomenological modelling choices and calibration targets. The key point is that CP outputs usually constrain model structure and parameter ranges; they rarely translate into one-to-one macroscopic parameters
rows: Directional uniaxial yield stresses and  r -values
Calibration of the initial anisotropic yield function and baseline directional hardening trends
Strongly influenced by the assumed texture statistics and by how macroscopic averaging is performed; they do not by themselves identify path-dependent hardening.
Plane-strain and equi-biaxial yield points; selected locus segments
Discrimination between simple Hill-type forms and advanced non-quadratic yield criteria
Sensitive to RVE size, boundary conditions and the convention used to define first yield or offset yield in the virtual test.
Yield loci evolved to fixed plastic work or strain levels
Evidence for whether evolving anisotropy or distortional hardening is structurally required
Dense virtual data can hide correlation and identifiability problems; a high-parameter macromodel may simply absorb CP model bias.
Reverse-loading curves and transient hardening after path changes
Screening of backstress, two-surface or distortional-hardening architectures
Reverse responses are not uniquely mapped to one macroscopic internal-variable set; slip-system hardening choices and rate regularisation also affect the result.
Sensitivity to texture, phase fraction and grain morphology
Model-family ranking, experimental-test prioritisation and robustness studies
Useful mainly for trends and comparative sensitivity; rarely a direct route to unique parameter values.
Full-field strain/stress heterogeneity and localisation patterns
Structural sanity check on whether a macromodel is missing essential mechanisms
Difficult to collapse into a small set of macroscopic internal variables; these outputs are usually diagnostic rather than directly calibrating.

tables.caption: Frequent numerical issues in the FE implementation of anisotropic hardening models and practical remedies. The table is intentionally diagnostic rather than exhaustive
rows: Elastic–plastic switching chatter
Very small increments, tight tolerances, non-smooth yield loci
Alternation between elastic and plastic branches; noisy incremental response
Use a robust yield tolerance, active-set logic and adaptive substepping near first yield. Confirm that the oscillation is not created by an oversized numerical viscosity.
Local Newton stagnation
Severe path change, poorly scaled residuals, strongly coupled backstress/distortional variables
Residual norm stalls or oscillates; excessive iteration count
Scale residual blocks, use a line search or damping strategy, and reparameterise internal variables if magnitudes differ by orders of magnitude.
Ill-conditioned local Jacobian or tangent
Reduced yield-surface curvature, repeated eigenvalues, incomplete linearisation
Loss of quadratic convergence; abrupt cutback requests from the global solver

Check derivative consistency, regularise near singular curvature states, and compare the hand-coded tangent against finite-difference or automatic-differentiation benchmarks at the material-point level.
Inadmissible parameter set
Unconstrained optimisation, over-flexible model family, poor initial guess
Non-convex yield locus, negative dissipation, algorithm breakdown

Impose admissibility constraints during optimisation, restrict the parameter space to structurally justified ranges, and reject parameter sets that fail convexity or dissipation checks before FE deployment.
Incomplete non-associated implementation
Yield function and plastic potential differentiated inconsistently
Correct stress levels but wrong plastic-flow direction or  r -value evolution; poor reverse-loading convergence
Linearise yield and plastic-potential derivatives separately and verify proportional, reverse, and orthogonal loading paths against a reference material-point implementation.
Plane-stress inconsistency
Thickness strain drift, shell/solid disagreement, unstable springback prediction
Solve plane stress and plastic consistency in one coupled local problem, and verify agreement between shell and solid benchmarks before production use.
Objective-rate or finite-strain mismatch
Porting the model between codes with different stress measures or corotational updates
Code-to-code disagreement under large rotation; spurious shear stress
Document the stress/strain measures and work-conjugacy assumptions explicitly; verify the same loading path in each target FE environment.
Artificial-viscosity dependence
Numerical rate regularisation too strong
Time-step-dependent hardening, loop shape or springback
Perform a viscosity and time-step sensitivity study and, if the response changes materially, treat the viscosity as a constitutive parameter requiring separate rate calibration.
Parameter non-identifiability masquerading as numerical failure
Too many parameters relative to the test matrix
Multiple local minima, unstable extrapolation, contradictory "best" fits
Reduce model freedom, calibrate in stages, add path-change data or CP-generated virtual data, and use multi-start optimisation with physically motivated parameter bounds.
